opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think that's one of the hardest parts of the problem, and it's often overlooked. People talk about "value alignment" as if there's a single set of human values we just need to write down and hand to the system. But there isn't. We have eight billion people, and we don't agree on religion, politics, ethics, economics, what a good life looks like. Even a single person isn't consistent; your values today aren't the same as ten years ago, and they shift depending on whether you're hungry or tired. So the target itself is moving and contradictory.

Philosophers have tried for thousands of years to come up with a universally accepted ethical framework, and we haven't succeeded. Now we're expecting computer scientists to solve it in a few years, encode it precisely, and make sure a system much smarter than us interprets it the way we intended and keeps it as it self-improves. Each of those steps is extremely difficult on its own.

If you try to aggregate everyone's preferences, you run into the problems social choice theory has known about for a long time. Voting systems have impossibility results. Some group always loses, and with a superintelligent system enforcing the outcome, losing could be permanent.

One idea I've written about is that instead of forcing everyone into one shared compromise, you could give each person their own virtual world, a personal universe, where their values are what gets satisfied. The multi-agent alignment problem becomes a lot of single-agent problems. You still have to align the system that runs the substrate all those universes live on, so it doesn't solve the core problem. But it changes the question from "how do we make eight billion people agree" to something that's at least conceptually more tractable.

My honest view is that we don't know how to do this, and I'm not sure it's solvable in principle. People get uncomfortable when I say that. But if we can't even define what we're aligning to, claiming we'll get it right on the first try with a system we can't fully understand or control seems very optimistic.

r001.rationale: The response says human values are diverse, inconsistent, and shifting, making the alignment target “moving and contradictory.”

r002.rationale: It questions how values can be precisely specified, noting that there is no single agreed set to write down and that expecting computer scientists to encode it precisely is extremely difficult.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think this is actually one of the places where the problem gets harder, not easier, the more you look at it. People talk about "aligning AI with human values" as if there's a thing called human values that we could point to. There isn't. We have eight billion people, and they disagree about almost everything that matters. They disagree about religion, about politics, about what a good life looks like, about whether it's acceptable to eat animals. Even one individual is not consistent over time. What I wanted at twenty is not what I want now, and what I want on Monday morning is different from what I want on Friday night.

So you have at least three separate problems stacked on top of each other. First, what does it even mean for values to be aligned? Nobody has a formal definition that survives contact with philosophy. Second, even if you pick one person and say, align it with Lex, we don't know how to do that technically. We can't verify that a system actually has the values we think we put in. Third, and this is the one you're asking about, whose values? Any choice you make is going to be unacceptable to a large fraction of humanity. If you average everybody out, you get something nobody actually wants. If you let the AI pick, you've given up control. If you let a company or a government pick, that's just a dictatorship with extra steps.

There are proposals. One idea I find interesting is that you don't need one aligned system, you need personal AIs, each one aligned with its individual user, and then you have a kind of negotiation layer on top, like we have between humans today. That at least preserves pluralism. But it reintroduces conflict, and now the conflict is between superintelligent agents, which is not obviously better.

And I think the honest answer is that we don't have a solution. What we have is a lot of people hoping that the problem will get solved somehow before the systems become capable enough that it matters. I'm not comfortable with that. If you can't define the target, you can't hit it, and you certainly can't prove you've hit it. That's why I keep saying this is not an engineering problem we can just work hard on and solve. Some aspects of it may be unsolvable in principle, and we should take that possibility seriously before we build something we can't undo.

r001.rationale: The response describes widespread disagreement and says any single choice would be unacceptable to many people, while averaging would produce something nobody wants. This conveys the apparent incompatibility of aligning AI with everyone’s differing values.

r002.rationale: The response says there is no formal definition of aligned values and that without defining the target, it cannot be hit or verified. This directly raises how an informal alignment goal could be specified precisely.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to distinguish between aligning AI with one person and aligning it with humanity. Those are very different problems. We don't have a solution to the first one, and the second one introduces conflicts that intelligence alone doesn't resolve.

People have genuinely incompatible preferences. It's not always a misunderstanding where, if we explain things better, everyone agrees. Sometimes one person wants precisely what another person wants to prevent. So what does it mean for a system to be aligned with both of them?

You can choose some aggregation procedure—majority vote, for example—but then you've made a moral and political choice about whose preferences count and how much. You haven't eliminated the problem. And whoever chooses that procedure has an enormous amount of power.

Then there's the fact that our values change. Do you align the system with what we want today, what we'll want tomorrow, or what it predicts we would want if we were better informed? Those can produce very different outcomes. So I don't think ‘align it with human values’ is a sufficiently precise specification. It's the beginning of the question.

r001.rationale: It describes people’s preferences as genuinely incompatible, including cases where one person wants what another wants to prevent, and asks how AI could be aligned with both.

r002.rationale: It says that “align it with human values” is not a sufficiently precise specification and treats it as an unresolved question.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two separate problems here. One is deciding what we want the system to be aligned with, and the other is figuring out how to make it reliably do that. We don’t have a solution to either one.

Humans disagree about values, sometimes fundamentally. Aligning a system with one person could make it dangerous to another person. Taking a majority vote doesn’t solve that; it can simply give the majority power over everyone else. And our values change over time, so even specifying the target is difficult.

You might try to give everyone a personal AI aligned with their own preferences, but then those systems interact, and the conflicts between people become conflicts between very capable machines. So personalization doesn’t eliminate the problem.

I would distinguish getting an AI to follow some instructions in a limited setting from guaranteeing that a superintelligent system will remain beneficial to humanity. The first can be useful and achievable. The second is a much stronger claim, and I don’t think we know how to establish it.

r001.rationale: It says humans can disagree fundamentally, that aligning with one person's values can make AI dangerous to another, and that majority voting can empower one group over others—presenting the goal as conflicting.

r002.rationale: It says choosing an alignment target is difficult because values differ and change, but it does not specifically question how informal notions like “good” or “desirable” could be formalized precisely.
